title: JESUS WAS ASKED FOR THE GREATEST COMMANDMENT. HIS ANSWER EXPOSES THE ONE THING MANY CHRISTIANS ARE STILL MISSING.
paragraphs: JESUS WAS ASKED FOR THE GREATEST COMMANDMENT. HIS ANSWER EXPOSES THE ONE THING MANY CHRISTIANS ARE STILL MISSING.

You can know the Bible, attend church, pray every day, give generously, and defend the truth… yet still overlook the very commandment Jesus called the greatest. And the most frightening part? You might not realize what is missing until you stand before the One you claim to love.
Not because it is complicated.
But because the answer is so simple that we have spent centuries finding ways to avoid what it demands.
What if the greatest danger to your spiritual life is not that you have stopped believing in God… but that you have learned how to practice Christianity without truly loving Him?
You know the songs.
You recognize the Scriptures.
You know when to say amen.
You might even be the person everyone calls when they need prayer.
But somewhere between the worship services, responsibilities, disappointments, unanswered prayers, and exhausting battles of ordinary life, something has quietly happened.
Your relationship with God has become a routine.
Your prayers have become requests.
Your obedience has become a checklist.
And the love that once made you weep in His presence has become something you remember more than something you experience.
You still believe.
You still show up.
But deep inside, there is a question you have been afraid to ask.
Lord… when did I become so busy doing things for You that I stopped simply loving You?
That question takes us straight into one of the most important conversations Jesus ever had.
And when we hear His answer in its original biblical context, we discover something far deeper than a religious slogan.
We discover the heartbeat of the entire Christian life.
In Mark 12:28, a scribe approaches Jesus after hearing Him answer a series of difficult questions. Unlike some of the other religious questioners, this man recognizes that Jesus has answered wisely.
So he asks:
“Which is the first commandment of all?” (Mark 12:28, KJV)
Imagine the weight of that moment.
The Law of Moses contained commandments governing worship, justice, holiness, family, relationships, and the daily life of God's people.
The question was not merely which commandment appeared first on a list.
It was which commandment stood above the others in importance.
Which one carried the greatest weight?
Which one revealed what God ultimately desired?
Jesus could have answered with an elaborate theological argument.
He could have discussed ceremonial purity, Sabbath observance, sacrifices, or the obligations of religious leaders.
Instead, He reached into the ancient Scriptures of Israel and spoke words that faithful Jewish people had treasured for generations.

“The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment.” (Mark 12:29–30, KJV)
Read that again.
Not just with your eyes.
With the part of your heart that knows what it feels like to love someone deeply.
Jesus did not say the greatest commandment was to become famous for God, impress people with your spirituality, accumulate religious achievements, or prove yourself worthy of heaven.
He said to love the Lord your God.
With all your heart.
All your soul.
All your mind.
All your strength.
Not a leftover corner of your life.
Not a convenient Sunday morning.
Not a few exhausted minutes before falling asleep.
All.
And that tiny word is where the commandment begins to search us.
Because many of us are willing to give God something.
But Jesus speaks of giving Him everything.
The words Jesus used were not new.
He was quoting Deuteronomy 6:4–5, a foundational confession of Israel's faith known as the Shema, named after its opening Hebrew word.
The ancient Hebrew begins:
שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
Shema Yisra'el, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad.
“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.” (Deuteronomy 6:4, KJV)
The written Hebrew contains the divine name represented by the four consonants YHWH. In reverent Jewish reading tradition, Adonai, meaning “Lord,” is spoken instead.
The opening word, שְׁמַע (shema), means “hear” or “listen.”
But in the covenant setting of Deuteronomy, this hearing is not intended to end with recognizing sounds or collecting information.
It calls God's people to listen attentively and respond faithfully.
This is important.
Because it is possible to hear a thousand sermons without allowing one command of God to transform your life.
It is possible to memorize verses about forgiveness while refusing to forgive.
It is possible to explain biblical holiness while secretly protecting the sin that is destroying your conscience.
It is possible to know what God says and still resist what He asks.
The problem is not always a lack of information.
Sometimes the problem is that our hearts have become skilled at listening without surrendering.
And the greatest commandment will not allow that comfortable distance.
The Hebrew of Deuteronomy 6:5 continues:
וְאָהַבְתָּ אֵת יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ בְּכָל־לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל־נַפְשְׁךָ וּבְכָל־מְאֹדֶךָ
Ve'ahavta et Adonai Elohekha, bekhol levavekha, uvekhol nafshekha, uvekhol me'odekha.
“And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.” (Deuteronomy 6:5, KJV)
The Hebrew word אָהַב (ahav) means “to love.”
But this love cannot be reduced to a passing emotion.
In the covenant relationship between God and His people, love includes loyalty, devotion, affection, and faithful obedience.
The Hebrew לֵבָב (levav), translated “heart,” refers not only to feelings but also to the inner person, including thoughts, desires, and decisions.
נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh), translated “soul,” can refer to one's life or living self.
And מְאֹד (me'od), translated “might,” ordinarily expresses the idea of “very” or “much,” but in this passage conveys the fullness of one's capacity and resources.
Jesus' wording in Mark, recorded in Greek, makes the comprehensive demand unmistakable:
ἀγαπήσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς διανοίας σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος σου.
Agapēseis kyrion ton theon sou ex holēs tēs kardias sou kai ex holēs tēs psychēs sou kai ex holēs tēs dianoias sou kai ex holēs tēs ischyos sou.
“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.” (Mark 12:30, translated from the Greek)
The Greek verb ἀγαπήσεις (agapēseis) comes from agapaō, meaning “to love.”
The word διάνοια (dianoia) refers to the mind or understanding, while ἰσχύς (ischys) refers to strength or power.
These are not four isolated compartments that must be measured separately.
Together, they emphasize total devotion.
Your inner life.
Your thinking.
Your desires.
Your abilities.
Your energy.
Your decisions.
Your very existence.
God is not asking for a carefully managed percentage of your affection.
He is worthy of your whole self.
And suddenly the greatest commandment becomes painfully personal.
Because it is easy to say, “I love Jesus.”
It is harder to ask whether that love shapes the way you speak to your spouse when you are angry.
Whether it changes how you treat the employee who cannot do anything for you.
Whether it affects what you watch when nobody is around.
Whether it changes how you handle money, temptation, resentment, pride, and the people who have wounded you.
Whether you still trust God's goodness when His answer is not the answer you desperately wanted.
Whether you love Him when following Him costs you something.
That is where religious language meets real discipleship.
Not in how loudly we announce our love.
But in whether that love is allowed to transform us.
Jesus said in John 14:15:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.” (KJV)
Notice what He did not say.
He did not say that obedience purchases His love.
He taught that obedience is a fitting expression of love for Him.
This distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because some believers have spent years trying to earn what can only be received by grace.
They pray because they are terrified God will abandon them.
They serve because they are afraid they will never be enough.
They give because they think God will withhold His blessing unless they prove their devotion.
They carry guilt like a permanent identity.
And eventually, they become exhausted.
Not necessarily because following Jesus is meaningless to them.
But because they have confused loving obedience with the impossible task of making themselves worthy of salvation.
Listen carefully.
The greatest commandment tells us what we owe God. The Gospel reveals what God has done for sinners who have failed to give Him what He deserves.
That is the difference between a religion built on human achievement and salvation received through Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired every broken part of our lives.
Not after we had stopped struggling.
Not after our prayers became eloquent or our church attendance became perfect.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
And grace, rightly understood, does not invite us to remain unchanged.
It calls us to repentance, faith, and a new life in Christ.
Think about Peter.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had heard the teachings.
He had boldly declared that he would remain faithful even if others fell away.
Then came the night of Jesus' arrest.
The pressure.
The fear.
The questions around a fire.
And the terrible words of denial.
Three times Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that the Lord turned and looked upon Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The eyes of the One he loved.
The memory of everything he had promised.
The crushing realization of what he had done.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Some of you understand that kind of grief.
Not because you denied Jesus in a courtyard.
But because you remember the promises you made to Him.
The habit you said you would abandon.
The relationship you knew was pulling you away from God.
The bitterness you promised to release.
The secret compromise you thought you had finally conquered.
And then you fell again.
Perhaps you have whispered, “Lord, how can I say I love You when I keep failing You?”
Peter's story does not end beside that fire.
After His resurrection, Jesus met His disciples by the Sea of Galilee.
And in John 21, He addressed Peter with a question that went deeper than Peter's public failure.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?” (John 21:16, KJV)
Jesus asked Peter about his love and commissioned him to care for His sheep.
Three times Jesus questioned Peter, and three times Peter affirmed his love.

There is a well-known distinction between the Greek verbs agapaō and phileō in this passage. Although these words can carry different shades of meaning, John's Gospel also uses them interchangeably in some contexts. We should therefore be careful not to build the entire meaning of Peter's restoration on an assumed difference between the two verbs.
The unmistakable message is powerful enough.
The risen Jesus confronted Peter's failure, drew out his confession of love, and entrusted him with responsibility.
Peter's denial was real.
His grief was real.
And Christ's restoring mercy was real.
Jesus did not pretend that the betrayal never happened.
He did not declare that obedience no longer mattered.
He restored a fallen disciple and called him to follow.
That is grace.
Not permission to keep walking toward destruction.
But mercy that calls a sinner back into fellowship and faithfulness.
Maybe you need to hear that today.
Your failure does not have to become the final chapter of your story.
The same Christ who restored Peter still calls sinners to repent and follow Him.
And perhaps the question confronting you today is not merely, “Have you failed?”
You already know the answer.
The deeper question is, “Will you return to the Savior who calls you?”
Because the greatest commandment is not simply about becoming a more disciplined religious person.
It is about loving the living God.
And that love must reach beyond ourselves.
Jesus did not stop after naming the first commandment.
He continued:
“And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. There is none other commandment greater than these.” (Mark 12:31, KJV)
He was quoting Leviticus 19:18.
The two commandments belong together.
Love God.
Love your neighbor.
In Matthew 22:40, Jesus says:
“On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” (KJV)
Everything the Law and the Prophets taught about faithful human response to God is bound up with these two commands.
Not because every commandment becomes unnecessary.
But because love for God and neighbor expresses the moral heart of what God requires.
And this is where the message becomes uncomfortable again.
Because some people are very passionate about defending biblical truth but remarkably careless about the people standing in front of them.
They can correct someone's theology in seconds.
But they struggle to show patience to their own children.
They can publicly condemn sin.
But they refuse to confess their own.
They can speak passionately about holiness.
But their words leave wounded people feeling despised rather than called toward the truth and mercy of Christ.
Truth matters.
Repentance matters.
Holiness matters.
But we cannot use those words as an excuse to abandon love.
First John 4:20 confronts this contradiction:
“If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar...” (KJV)
Those words should humble all of us.
Because the greatest commandment is not fulfilled by impressive religious language while our relationships remain untouched by grace.
Love does not mean approving every choice someone makes.
Jesus loved sinners without calling sin righteousness.
He offered mercy while calling people to repentance.
He spoke truth without compromising the Father's will.
And at the cross, we see both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable depth of divine love.
The cross is not proof that sin does not matter.
It is proof that sin matters so much that our redemption required the sacrifice of the Son of God.
And love is so great that the Son willingly gave Himself.
First John 4:10 says:
“Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.” (KJV)
There it is.
The foundation of everything.
Not that we loved God first.
But that He loved us.
The Greek word translated “propitiation” in this verse is ἱλασμός (hilasmos), referring to Christ's atoning sacrifice for sins.
Our hope is not that our love has been flawless.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ is the sufficient Savior of sinners.
And because He first loved us, we are called to love Him in return.
Not to purchase salvation.
Not to manipulate God.
Not to earn a place at His table.
But because His grace has opened the way for us to belong to Him.
Ephesians 2:8–10 brings both truths together.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace saves.
And saving grace produces a transformed life.
This is why love cannot remain a sentimental idea.
Real love begins to change what we treasure.
It changes what we pursue.
It changes what we are willing to surrender.
Sometimes it means turning away from a sin that has felt like your only comfort.
Sometimes it means apologizing to someone you have spent years blaming.
Sometimes it means praying for a person you would rather never see again.
Sometimes it means choosing honesty when a lie would be easier.
Sometimes it means continuing to trust God through grief that has left you with more questions than answers.
And sometimes it means coming before Jesus without any impressive words at all.
Just tears.
Just repentance.
Just a weary heart saying:
Lord, I have loved so many things more than You.
I have pursued approval more than Your presence.
I have protected my pride more than I have pursued peace.
I have treated Your mercy as something ordinary.
Please forgive me.
That is not a prayer of spiritual defeat.
It can be the beginning of genuine repentance.
And repentance is not merely feeling bad about what we have done.
It is turning from sin toward God.
The New Testament uses the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, carrying the idea of a change of mind or heart that involves a changed direction.
Repentance is not pretending the past never happened.
It is bringing our sins into the light and turning toward the mercy and lordship of Jesus Christ.
And there is something beautiful about a Savior who calls us to love Him with everything while knowing how deeply we need His grace.
He knows our weakness.
He knows our wandering.
He knows how easily fear can overtake faith.
He knows how quickly our attention can become captured by things that cannot save us.
Yet His invitation remains.
Come to Him.
Believe in Him.
Follow Him.
Love Him.
And let that love shape how you live.
Perhaps you have been trying to find your way back to God through religious performance.
You promised yourself you would pray longer.
Read more chapters.
Attend more services.
Give more money.
Volunteer more hours.
Some of those things can be beautiful expressions of faith.
But none of them can replace the Savior.
And none of them can buy His grace.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That principle matters whenever we talk about supporting Gospel work.
A believer with very little money can love Christ with extraordinary faithfulness.
A wealthy person can give generously and still need to examine the condition of the heart.
The widow whom Jesus observed giving two small coins in Mark 12:41–44 reminds us that God sees far more than the visible amount of an offering.
He sees the person.
He sees the sacrifice.
He sees what others overlook.
So when we invite people to help spread the Gospel, that invitation should never become a spiritual threat.
It should be an opportunity for willing partnership.
And that is part of the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
We believe the Word of God deserves to be shared, studied, understood, and lived.
Not merely quoted in passing.
Not reduced to a slogan.
But allowed to confront our pride, comfort our grief, expose our sin, strengthen our faith, and continually direct us to Jesus Christ.
We want the struggling believer to find encouragement.
The searching soul to encounter biblical truth.
The wounded Christian to remember the mercy of Jesus.
The spiritually complacent to be awakened to the seriousness and beauty of following Him.
And the person who has never truly understood the Gospel to discover that forgiveness and eternal life are found in Christ.
This work requires time, effort, resources, and faithful support.
It is simply one meaningful way to participate in sharing the message of Christ.
But the greatest value of supporting Gospel work will never be merchandise.
It is the opportunity to help make biblical truth accessible to someone who needs it.
Perhaps someone who has not opened a Bible in years.
Perhaps someone quietly fighting despair.
Perhaps someone who has mistaken religion for a relationship with Christ.
Perhaps someone who needs to hear the same truth you needed today.
You are still welcome here.
You can pray for the ministry.
You can read and share the free resources.
You can invite others to study the Word.
You can help someone encounter the Gospel simply by sending a message that says, “I thought of you when I read this.”
And sometimes a friend you thought was doing fine is quietly praying for God to send them a reason not to give up.
Not to impress anyone with your faith.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Not for a polished religious answer.
Not for something you think other Christians want to hear.
But for an honest response before God.
What has been competing with your love for Jesus lately?
Has it been fear?
Your career?
A relationship?
Unforgiveness?
The need to be accepted?
A hidden sin?
Your own exhaustion?
Or perhaps you have been so wounded by life that loving God has begun to feel difficult.
You might simply comment, “Lord, teach me to love You with all my heart.”
Or, if you are struggling and would welcome prayer, comment, “Pray for me. I want to come closer to Jesus.”
Because the greatest commandment was never intended to be admired from a distance.
It was meant to be lived.
But there is one final detail in Jesus' conversation with the scribe that we must not overlook.
After hearing Jesus' answer, the scribe agreed that loving God with the whole heart and loving one's neighbor as oneself was more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.
Jesus saw that he had answered wisely.
And then He said something remarkable:
“Thou art not far from the kingdom of God.” (Mark 12:34, KJV)
Not far.
Those two words are both encouraging and sobering.
The man had understood something essential.
He recognized the supreme importance of love for God and neighbor.
But Jesus did not say that intellectual understanding alone had brought him into the kingdom.
He said he was not far.
And perhaps that is where some readers find themselves today.
Not far.
You know the stories.
You understand the commandments.
You agree that Jesus taught the truth.
You recognize that your life needs to change.
But knowing about the kingdom is not the same as entering it.
Knowing the language of faith is not the same as personally trusting Christ.
And understanding the greatest commandment does not mean you have fulfilled it.
In fact, the more seriously we consider this commandment, the more clearly we see our need for a Savior.
Who among us has loved God perfectly with every thought, every desire, every decision, and every moment of strength?
Who has loved every neighbor as faithfully as God requires?
Our failure exposes our sin.
And our sin reveals why we need Jesus.
He did not come merely to give us a more inspiring moral standard.
He came to save sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Jesus Himself declared in Mark 1:15:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
That is the invitation.
Not to pretend you are already righteous.
Not to promise that you will never struggle again.
Not to purchase forgiveness through religious activity.
But to turn to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith, trusting His finished work rather than your own achievements.
And from that place of grace, to begin learning what it means to love Him with your whole life.
Maybe your love has grown cold.
Return to Him.
Maybe you have been hiding behind religious activity.
Come into the light.
Maybe you have wandered into sin.
Repent and turn to Christ.
Maybe you have been wounded so deeply that you barely know how to pray.
Bring your honest heart to Him.
Maybe you are beginning to realize that you have loved the blessings of God more than God Himself.
Confess it.
He already knows.
And the Gospel gives us reason to seek His mercy rather than run from His presence.
You can pray something like this, sincerely and in your own words:

Lord Jesus, I confess that I have not loved God with all my heart, soul, mind, and strength. I have sinned in ways I can see and in ways I have tried to ignore. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. I turn from my sin and place my trust in You. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to love You faithfully. Help me love others as You have commanded. Let my life bring glory to Your name. Amen.
A prayer is not a magical formula that saves because the correct words were spoken.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ, received through genuine faith, not in the performance of a religious ritual.
And following Him is not meant to be a solitary journey.
Remain close to Scripture.
Pray honestly.
Become rooted in a faithful local church where God's Word is taught.
Seek fellowship, accountability, and opportunities to serve.
Keep learning.
Keep repenting when you sin.
Keep looking to Christ.
Because Christian maturity is not becoming someone who no longer needs grace.
It is growing in love, holiness, humility, and dependence on the Savior who has shown us grace.
And one day, when the arguments, distractions, achievements, and anxieties of this passing world have faded, the greatest commandment will still remind us what mattered.
Not how many people applauded us.
Not how impressive our religious reputation became.
Not how successfully we appeared to have everything together.
But whether our lives were turned toward the God who is worthy of all our love.
That is why this question matters so deeply.
What was Jesus' greatest commandment?
To love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength.
And the second is to love your neighbor as yourself.
Simple enough to remember.
Deep enough to search a lifetime.
Impossible for sinful humanity to fulfill perfectly apart from the righteousness we need in Christ.
And beautiful enough that, through His grace, we can spend our lives learning to obey it.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, consider putting down your phone for a moment.
Not because God is waiting to condemn you for being distracted.
But because perhaps your heart needs to remember the One who loved you before you ever knew how to love Him.
You do not need a stage.
You do not need an audience.
You do not need impressive words.
You can simply turn toward Him.
And say:
Jesus, I have given my heart to so many things that could never save me.
Teach me to love You above them all.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not a platform.
Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who calls us to love God completely.
The One who loved us when we were sinners.
The One whose grace does not excuse our rebellion but calls us out of it.
The One who restores the repentant and makes all things new.
And if you remember only one thing from everything you have read, let it be this:
The greatest tragedy is not that you once failed to love Jesus as you should—it is to hear His call today and keep giving your heart to everything but Him.
